# Volume 4 — CHAPTER 28 ODDS AND ENDS

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“I’ve been looking through the death announcements,” Miss Winifred remarked, putting the Daily Enterprise aside and picking up her needlework.
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0000 }

Beneath a grim November sky, the harbor stretched out dark and gloomy, and dripping, lifeless leaves stuck thoroughly soaked to the window sills; nevertheless, the small house shone cheerful with the glow of a fire and seemed like springtime owing to the geraniums and ferns of Nell.
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0001 }

“In this place, it is perpetually summer, Nell,” Lorna had remarked on a certain day; and everyone who stayed as a guest in that home of dreams experienced the identical feeling.
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0002 }

“The Enterprise appears to specialize in death notices lately,” remarked Miss Winifred. “There are always two or three columns dedicated to them, and I do not miss a word. Reading them serves as a type of enjoyment for me, particularly if they include some home-made verse. I have found an exquisite example to show you:
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0003 }

She has departed to reside with her Creator, never again to wander. It was her custom to joyfully play and sing the hymn of Home, Sweet Home.
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0004 }

Who claims that our Island lacks all poetic skill! Nell, my dear, have you ever paid attention to how many wonderful individuals pass away? It is rather tragic. Within this paper are ten death notices, and each single one portrays a saint and a role model, including the men. This one covers old Peter Stimson, who has "left a large circle of friends to mourn his untimely loss." Good heavens, Nell, my dear, that individual had reached eighty, and anyone acquainted with him had been praying for his demise for the past thirty years. Go through the death notices whenever you feel down, Nell, my dear—most of all the notices for people you are familiar with. Provided you possess even the slightest sense of humor, they are bound to lift your spirits, trust ME. I only desire that I were tasked with composing the death notices for particular folks. Does not "obituary" strike you as a dreadfully hideous term? That precise Peter I was mentioning possessed a countenance that mirrored the term precisely. I could not glance at it without instantly remembering the word OBITUARY on the spot. I am aware of just one single term that is more hideous, and that term is RELICT. Good heavens, Nell, my dear, I might end up a spinster, yet it offers this reassurance—I shall never become the "relict" of any man.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0005 }

“It IS an ugly word,” Nell said with a laugh. “The cemetery in Brierley had a great number of aged gravestones that read 'sacred to the memory of So-and-So, RELICT of the late So-and-So.’ That phrase constantly brought to my mind a thing that was threadbare and damaged by moths. For what reason do a vast amount of terms associated with dying sound so unpleasant? I really desire that the habit of referring to a corpse as 'the remains’ might be done away with. A genuine shudder goes through me whenever the funeral director announces during a service, 'All who wish to see the remains please step this way.’ That statement constantly leaves me with the ghastly feeling that I am about to look upon the location of a cannibalistic banquet.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0006 }

“Indeed, my sole desire,” Miss Winifred remarked placidly, “is for no one to refer to me as 'our departed sister’ after my passing. My aversion to this constant referencing of sisters and brothers began half a decade back, during a itinerant preacher’s revival at the Glen. Right from the beginning, I had no time for the man. My gut told me he was untrustworthy. Which proved true. You see, he claimed to belong to the Presbyterian faith—though he pronounced it PresbyTARian—when he was actually a Methodist the whole time. Everyone was addressed by him as a brother or sister. That fellow possessed an extensive kin group. Squeezing my hand with great passion one evening, he begged, 'My DEAR sister Tolley, have you found Christ?’ After giving him a brief inspection, I responded coolly, 'MR. Fiske, my lone brother passed away fifteen years back, and I’ve taken on no new ones since then. Regarding my Christian faith, I trust and believe I possessed it while you were still a toddler wearing petticoats.’ That put an end to his talking, you may be sure. Understand, my sweet Nell, I do not despise every evangelist. Outstanding, sincere individuals have come here, accomplishing much good and causing ancient sinners to tremble. Yet this Fiske fellow was not among their number. One night, I enjoyed a quiet chuckle on my own. Fiske requested that every Christian rise. Rest assured, I remained seated! Such displays have never appealed to me. However, the majority stood up, after which he requested that everyone desiring to become a Christian stand. When no one moved for a bit, Fiske began singing a hymn as loudly as he could. Sitting right ahead of me in the Millison family bench was wretched little Ikey Pratt. As a ten-year-old placed child, he was pushed to absolute exhaustion by Millison. Because the miserable little boy was perpetually exhausted, he dropped off instantly whenever he attended service or found a spot to sit quietly for a short while. Throughout the revival, he had been resting, and I was glad the unfortunate child was obtaining a reprieve, you can be sure. Now, as Fiske’s singing rose toward the heavens and the congregation joined the song, unfortunate Ikey jerked awake. Imagining it was merely a typical hymn where everyone was expected to rise, he jumped to his feet with great haste, aware that Maria Millison would scold him severely for napping during the service. Catching sight of him, Fiske paused and yelled, 'A further soul brought to light! Glory Hallelujah!’ Yet there stood miserable, terrified Ikey, barely conscious and yawning, with no thought whatsoever for his soul. Unfortunate kid, he lacked the leisure to focus on anything beyond his exhausted, overburdened small frame.
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0007 }

“Lorna attended one evening, and the Fiske-man pursued her immediately—oh, he took a particular interest in the salvation of the attractive young women, trust me!—and he injured her feelings to the extent that she refused to return. Subsequently, he offered prayers aloud every single night, right before everyone, asking the Lord to soften her stubborn heart. At last, I approached Mr. Leavitt, who was our pastor at the time, and warned him that unless he ordered Fiske to cease, I would stand up the following evening and launch my hymn book at his head whenever he referred to that 'beautiful but unrepentant young woman.’ I certainly would have executed it, trust ME. Mr. Leavitt brought a halt to it, yet Fiske persisted with his assemblies until Charley Fairlie terminated his work in the Glen. Mrs. Charley had spent the entire winter away in California. She had suffered from severe depression during the autumn—a spiritual depression—which was a trait in her ancestry. Her father experienced such intense distress over the conviction that he was guilty of the unforgivable sin that he passed away in the asylum. Consequently, when Rose Fairlie developed those symptoms, Charley sent her away to stay with her sister located in Los Angeles. She recovered completely and returned home at the exact moment the Fiske revival reached its peak. She disembarked from the train at the Glen, looking quite cheerful and happy, and the very first sight that confronted her on the dark, gable-end of the freight shed was the query, painted in huge white characters two feet tall, 'Whither goest thou—to heaven or hell?’ That concept had originated with Fiske, who had hired Henry Rudge to execute the painting. Rose merely let out a scream and collapsed into a faint; and once she was brought back home, her condition deteriorated beyond before. Charley Fairlie approached Mr. Leavitt and stated that every member of the Fairlie family would abandon the congregation if Fiske remained any longer. Mr. Leavitt was forced to yield, since the Fairlies provided fifty percent of his stipend, so Fiske left, leaving us to rely on our Bibles again for guidance on reaching heaven. Following his departure, Mr. Leavitt discovered that the man was merely a Methodist in disguise, which made him feel quite ill, trust ME. Mr. Leavitt had his flaws in certain areas, but he remained a solid, genuine Presbyterian.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0008 }

“Incidentally, yesterday I received a letter from Mr. Treleaven,” Nell remarked. “He requested that I send you his kind regards.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0009 }

“I do not desire his tokens,” Miss Winifred stated sharply.
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0010 }

“For what reason?” Nell asked, thoroughly surprised. “It was my belief that he was to your liking.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0011 }

“Indeed, I did so, after a fashion. However, what he did to Lorna is something I will never pardon him for. That poor girl is grieving over him—as though she had not already suffered sufficient distress—while he is undoubtedly roaming about Toronto, having a good time just as he always does. That is precisely how a man acts.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0012 }

“Oh, Miss Winifred, in what way did you discover this?”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0013 }

“Goodness, Nell, my love, don’t I possess eyes? Besides, Lorna has been known to me from the time she was an infant. Throughout this past autumn, a different sort of sorrow has been visible in her gaze, and I am certain that author fellow was somehow responsible for it. Making myself the instrument that brought him to this place is something I will always regret. However, I did not anticipate he would turn out as he did. My expectation was merely that he would resemble the previous gentlemen Lorna had taken in as boarders—arrogant young fools, the whole lot of them, for whom she had no time whatsoever. Indeed, a single one among them attempted to flirt with her on one occasion, and she gave him such a cold reception that I am confident he has failed to warm up ever since. Consequently, the idea of any peril never crossed my mind.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0014 }

“Do not allow Lorna to think that you are aware of her secret,” Nell said hastily. “It would cause her pain, I believe.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0015 }

“Have faith in me, my dear Nell. My life did not start yesterday. Oh, may every man be cursed! To start with, Lorna’s existence was destroyed by one of them, and currently a different member of that brood arrives and leaves her even more miserable. Believe me, Nell, this earth is a terrible location.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0016 }

“There is a thing on earth awry Will be explained in due course,”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0017 }

recited Nell in a dreamy manner.
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0018 }

“Should that happen, it will occur in a realm devoid of men,” Miss Winifred remarked despondently.
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0019 }

Hugh came inside and inquired, “In what way have the crew misbehaved this time?”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0020 }

“Trouble—trouble! What other thing have they ever accomplished?”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0021 }

“Eve was the one who ate the apple, Miss Winifred.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0022 }

“A male creature was the one who lured her,” Miss Winifred shot back victoriously.
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0023 }

Once her initial agony had passed, Lorna discovered she could continue living despite everything, much like the majority of people, regardless of the specific nature of their suffering. She may have even taken pleasure in certain times, being part of the cheerful group within the small house of dreams. Yet, had Nell harbored any expectation that Adrian Treleaven was fading from her memory, the secret longing in Lorna’s gaze at any reference to his name would have disabused her of the idea. Moved to pity by that longing, Nell consistently managed to share fragments of information from Adrian’s correspondence with Captain Saul or Hugh while Lorna was present. The way the girl reddened and drained of color during these instances made the intensity of her feelings painfully clear. Nevertheless, she abstained from discussing him with Nell, nor did she ever refer to that evening on the sand-bar.
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0024 }

Her aged canine passed away on a certain day, causing her to mourn his loss deeply.
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0025 }

“He has been my friend for such a long time,” she said to Nell with sorrow. “You know, he was Rufus’s old dog—Rufus owned him for about a year before our marriage. He entrusted him to me upon sailing on the Four Sisters. Carlo grew very attached to me—and the affection of that dog sustained me during that initial terrible year following mother's death, when I was on my own. Hearing that Rufus was returning made me fear Carlo would no longer belong so much to me. Yet he appeared to care nothing for Rufus, despite having loved him so much previously. As if he were a stranger, he would snap and growl at him. I felt glad. Having a single creature whose love belonged entirely to me was sweet. Nell, that old dog provided me with such comfort. Because he became so weak during the fall, I feared his life would end soon—nevertheless, I harbored hopes of nursing him through the winter. This morning he appeared fairly healthy. As he lay on the rug in front of the fire, he suddenly stood up and slunk over to my side; placing his head on my lap, he bestowed one affectionate glance upon me from his large, gentle, canine eyes—and right after that, he simply trembled and passed away. I will miss him greatly.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0026 }

“Allow me to bestow upon you a different hound, Lorna,” Nell uttered. “A beautiful Lindsay setter is coming to me as a Yule gift intended for Hugh. Allow me to bestow one upon you as well.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0027 }

Lorna gave a shake of her head.
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0028 }

“I would rather not at this moment, I appreciate it, Nell. Taking on a new dog is not something I am up for right now. My capacity to care for a replacement feels completely exhausted. Maybe—eventually—I will accept one from you. Having a dog is actually necessary for me as a form of defense. However, Carlo possessed qualities that were nearly human—replacing him too quickly just would not be APPROPRIATE, poor faithful boy.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0029 }

Seven days prior to Christmas, Nell traveled to Brierley, remaining there past the festive season. Hugh arrived to collect her, leading to a joyful New Year's party at Grey Shutters, where Pembrokes, Carrows, and Ducketts gathered together to feast upon a meal that Mrs. Agatha and Thirza had planned and prepared with great diligence. Upon their return to Seven Gulls, the small dwelling was nearly buried by snow, as the third tempest of a season destined to be exceptionally severe had swept up the harbor, piling massive drifts against every obstacle in its path. Nevertheless, Captain Saul had cleared the pathways and doorways with his shovel, while Miss Winifred had visited to start a fire upon the hearth.
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0030 }

“My dear Nell, I am happy to see you return! However, have you ever beheld drifts like these? The Vane place is completely hidden from view unless one ascends to the second floor. Lorna will be thrilled at your return. She is practically interred over there. Thankfully, Rufus is able to clear the snow with a shovel and finds it very entertaining. Tabitha relayed a message asking me to inform you that she will be available tomorrow. To what destination are you headed now, Captain?”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0031 }

“I think I’m going to make my way up to the Glen so I can keep old Martin Strong company for a while. His death is approaching, and he feels lonely. Since he spent his whole life working too hard to form relationships, he lacks many friends. Nevertheless, he has accumulated a great deal of wealth.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0032 }

“Well, he reasoned that as he was unable to serve both God and Mammon, sticking to Mammon was his best choice,” Miss Winifred stated sharply. “Because of that, he ought not to grumble if he currently finds Mammon’s companionship lacking.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0033 }

Captain Saul stepped outside, yet he recalled a detail in the yard and briefly returned.
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0034 }

“A letter reached me from Mr. Treleaven, Mistress Carrow, in which he states that the life-book has been accepted and will be printed coming autumn. Obtaining this information made me feel truly joyous. The thought that I shall finally view it in print fills my mind.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0035 }

“That person is utterly insane regarding his life-book,” Miss Winifred remarked with pity. “As for me, I believe the world already contains way too many books.”
{: #nw-v04-c28-p0036 }
